Your 2026 Rights + Step-by-Step Scripts By Jonathan Velez , Personal Finance Writer & Editor · Reviewed against primary sources · Updated October 29, 2026 Skip to your cancellation plan If you can't cancel a subscription, identify the actual biller and how you signed up, then send a dated request through that company's verified cancellation route. Keep proof of each attempt, and take any charges that continue to the proper provider or regulator. To build your plan, the planner below asks four questions: the service, who bills you or where you signed up, your state or city, and what happened when you tried to cancel. It returns a next action, plus an official provider path when your answers match a verified source. You also get the federal baseline, a note for California, Colorado, Maine, New York State or New York City (or a notice that no specific example matched), a script to copy and edit, proof reminders and escalation links. Your answers stay in your browser tab, and the planner does not collect your name, account, payment or contact details. Federal baseline For covered internet transactions with a negative-option feature, ROSCA requires material-term disclosure, express informed consent and a simple way to stop recurring charges. It does not promise one-click cancellation for every subscription. Find the Company That Bills You The company that bills you controls the cancellation route, and that company can differ from the brand you watch or use. If Apple bills you, cancel through Apple's subscription settings , which handle only Apple-billed subscriptions. If Google Play bills you, cancel in Google Play , because deleting the app does not cancel the subscription. If Roku bills you, use Roku's subscription page . Otherwise, use the provider's own route. Netflix separates direct Netflix billing from partner billing, and signing out or deleting the app does not cancel. AT&T publishes separate cancellation help for wireless and internet service, and account ownership and equipment-return steps vary. ADT's Blue by ADT help page says deleting the app account does not cancel monitoring. Crunch's FAQ says some clubs support online cancellation, while other members may need to contact or visit their home club. The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) consumer advice also tells you to record the terms, identify the actual biller and watch your charges. What the Federal Rule Change Means The FTC's 2024 click-to-cancel amendments to its Negative Option Rule are not in effect, because a federal appeals court vacated them on procedural grounds. The United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit found the FTC had skipped a preliminary regulatory analysis that a statute requires. The court did not rule on the merits, and the federal framework was not abolished. The FTC's February 2026 Federal Register notice changed the rule text to match the ruling and restored the pre-2024 text. That notice is not a new click-to-cancel law. The FTC's Negative Option Rule page records a March 11, 2026 advance notice of proposed rulemaking (ANPRM) seeking comment on possible amendments, and an ANPRM is not binding law. The Restore Online Shoppers' Confidence Act (ROSCA) still applies to covered internet transactions with a negative-option feature. For those transactions, the seller must disclose material terms before taking billing information, get your express informed consent and give you a simple way to stop recurring charges. ROSCA does not create a one-click or same-channel cancellation rule for every subscription. If the FTC adopts amendments after the ANPRM, the federal baseline in the planner would change. State and NYC Protections: Selected Examples Some state and city laws add cancellation rules, and each one depends on coverage, dates and exceptions. The planner shows these as selected examples and does not survey every state. California's Automatic Renewal Law amendments took effect July 1, 2025, with consent and cancellation requirements for covered offers, including online cancellation where a covered enrollment was online. Colorado Senate Bill (SB) 25-145 sets channel-specific cancellation requirements for covered offers and renewals beginning February 16, 2026, based on how and when the contract was offered or renewed. Maine's Title 10, section 1210-C covers listed automatic renewals for online media players, mobile apps, online software and health-club memberships, and covered sellers must accept cancellation by the same method and manner as signup. New York General Business Law (GBL) § 527-a requires an easy cancellation mechanism through the same medium, plus other methods, for covered renewal offers, and it bars obstruction or unreasonable delay. GBL § 527-a exempts licensed security-system alarm operators and other specified businesses, so it may not help with an ADT monitoring contract where that exemption applies. GBL § 624 gives health-club members cancellation rights in specific circumstances, including a three-business-day right in covered contracts. GBL § 624 does not let you cancel every gym contract at any time. The New York City (NYC) Click-to-Cancel rule is effective October 1, 2026, and for covered offers it requires cancellation through the same medium you used to consent. The NYC rule also prohibits obstruction or unreasonable delay, and it exempts licensed alarm operators and other listed categories. The planner cannot decide whether one of these laws covers your contract, so read the coverage and exception language in the linked statute or rule. Use These Scripts and Keep Proof A written request can say: "I am canceling my [service] on account [account number], effective [date]. Please confirm in writing the cancellation, the effective date, any final balance and any equipment I need to return." On a call, ask for those same four items and a confirmation number before you hang up. Save screenshots of the cancellation page, plus emails, chat transcripts and confirmation numbers. For each call, write down the date, the time and the representative's name. If AT&T or another provider asks you to return equipment, keep the shipping receipt with your cancellation record. The planner's copy button copies a generic script with placeholders, so fill in your own account details before you send it. If Charges Continue After You Ask If charges continue after you ask to cancel, contact the company that bills you again and send your dated proof. FTC ReportFraud accepts reports of suspected deceptive or unfair business practices, but a report does not settle a private contract dispute or guarantee a refund. For communications-service problems within its scope, you can file with the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) , and its jurisdiction varies. In New York City, the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection (DCWP) offers a Click-to-Cancel summary and complaint route. Filing a DCWP complaint does not guarantee an individual resolution. After Cancellation: Check the Next Statement Match each recurring charge on your card or bank statement to its biller, and file the cancellation confirmation once the charge is gone. For a wider review of recurring charges, read the section "Subscription Creep: The Quiet Budget Killer" in the guide to budgeting for teens and college students . If the charge appears again, open the planner, choose charged after cancellation, and send your dated proof to the biller before you file with the matching regulator. Two Hypothetical Paths Through the Planner This is a hypothetical path through the planner, used to show how the route map works; it describes no real account or measured result. Suppose a reader in a state the planner does not list pays for a streaming service through Google Play and was charged again after asking to cancel. That reader would choose Netflix or other streaming, Google Play as the biller, Other or unknown for location, and Charged after cancellation. The plan would point to Google Play's cancellation route and show the ROSCA baseline. It would also say that no specific state example matched, then give a script, proof reminders and escalation links for continued charges. A second hypothetical reader in New York City has ADT monitoring and was blocked when trying to cancel. Before relying on the NYC rule, that reader should note that both the NYC rule and GBL § 527-a exempt licensed alarm operators. The same reader should also know that ADT's help page says deleting the Blue by ADT app account does not cancel monitoring. Common Cancellation Mistakes Deleting the app and assuming the subscription ended. Netflix and Google Play both say deleting the app does not cancel. Deleting a Blue by ADT app account and expecting monitoring to stop. Asking the streaming brand to cancel when Apple, Google Play, Roku or a partner is the actual biller. Canceling by phone without writing down the date, the representative's name and a confirmation number. Treating the FTC's 2024 click-to-cancel amendments as current law after the Eighth Circuit vacated them. Relying on New York's renewal law or the NYC rule for alarm monitoring when the licensed alarm operator exemption applies. Frequently Asked Questions Can I cancel a subscription straight away? No law on this page gives an instant cancellation right for every subscription. ROSCA requires a simple way to stop recurring charges for covered internet transactions, and some state and city laws add rules for covered offers. New York's health-club law includes a three-business-day right only in covered contracts. Ask the biller in writing for the effective date and any final balance. How do I cancel streaming channels? Cancel streaming channels through the company that bills you. Use Roku's subscription page if Roku bills you, Apple or Google Play if either one bills you, and the streaming service's own route otherwise. Netflix separates direct billing from partner billing and says signing out or deleting the app does not cancel. How do I force cancel a subscription? No single step forces a company to cancel. Send a dated written request through the biller's verified route, ask for written confirmation and keep proof. If charges continue, report them to FTC ReportFraud , to the FCC for communications services within its scope, or to NYC DCWP in New York City. A report or complaint does not guarantee a refund or an individual resolution. How do I find all my streaming subscriptions? Streaming subscriptions may be billed by Apple, Google Play, Roku, another partner or the service itself. Apple subscription instructions , Google Play subscription instructions and Roku subscription instructions explain those billing routes. A card or bank statement can identify services that bill you directly. The FTC's consumer advice also explains how to identify the biller. Why is it so hard to cancel subscriptions? Signup, billing and service can sit with different companies, and each company publishes its own cancellation steps. Netflix can be billed directly or through a partner, AT&T splits wireless and internet cancellation, and Crunch members may need to contact or visit their home club. The FTC's 2024 click-to-cancel amendments were vacated, so the same-medium rules on this page come from selected state and city laws, each with its own coverage and exceptions. Learning how to make a budget in this order means you pick a method like 50/30/20 or zero-based after you know what comes in and what goes out. The four steps come from the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) , which offers a tool for each one. You can start the first step today with your latest pay stub and a notepad. Tools for this journey Monthly Budget Calculator → 50/30/20 Budget Calculator → Zero-Based Budget Calculator → The Four Steps to Build a Budget from Scratch A budget gets built in four steps, and the first three steps each answer a question the CFPB asks: Where does my money come from? Write down every source of income, including pay from each job, self-employment income, child support and government benefits. The CFPB offers an Income Tracker for this step. Where does my money go? Log your spending for a month and sort it into categories, so you can see what a typical month costs you. The CFPB offers a Spending Tracker for this step. What are all my bills and when are they due? Put every bill on a calendar by its due date. The CFPB offers a Bill Calendar to track due dates and spot tight weeks. Create your working budget. Combine your income, your spending and your bill timing into one realistic plan. Start step 1 today. Pull your latest pay stub and any benefit or support statements, then write down each amount and the date it arrives. Step 2 needs a full month of records. Do them in order anyway, since step 4 only works when it is built from the numbers you collected in steps 1 to 3. Where the Numbers Come from When You Make a Budget The spending numbers in your budget should come from a month of real bank and card statements rather than from memory. Download the last full month from every checking account and credit card you use. Copy each charge into a category such as housing, groceries, transport, debt payments or fun. If a full month of statements feels overwhelming, the CFPB suggests reviewing your expenses one week at a time. Four weekly sessions cover the same month of spending in smaller pieces. Pick one evening a week and finish one week of charges in that sitting. For income, write down take-home pay, the amount that lands in your account after deductions. The 50/30/20 split covered below is a share of take-home pay, so using a larger pre-deduction figure would make every share too big. If your pay changes from month to month, step 1 needs a different approach, and our guide on how to budget with irregular income walks through it. If a recurring charge is one you want to stop, use the subscription cancellation planner to identify the biller and keep a dated record. Choosing Between 50/30/20 and Zero-Based Budgets A 50/30/20 budget splits take-home pay into three fixed shares, while a zero-based budget assigns every dollar of income a job until nothing is left unassigned. Both methods need the numbers from the four steps above. Pick one after step 2, once you know what a real month costs. Under 50/30/20, 50% of take-home pay goes to needs, 30% to wants and 20% to savings and debt payments beyond the minimums. For example, a hypothetical take-home pay of $4,000 a month splits into $2,000 for needs, $1,200 for wants and $800 for savings and extra debt payments ($4,000 x 0.50, 0.30 and 0.20). You can run your own figure through the 50/30/20 Budget Calculator . A zero-based budget gives the same hypothetical $4,000 a list of jobs instead of three shares. One version might look like this: $2,150 for housing and bills $600 for groceries and transport $350 for minimum debt payments $400 for wants $500 for savings Those five amounts add up to $4,000, so income minus assignments equals zero. Your own figures will differ, and the Zero-Based Budget Calculator does the subtraction for you. The two examples show how needs can pass 50% of take-home pay. If you count groceries, transport and minimum payments as needs, the zero-based household spends $3,100 on needs ($2,150 + $600 + $350). That is 77.5% of $4,000, or $1,100 more than the $2,000 needs share under 50/30/20. High housing costs or heavy debt can push your needs past 50% the same way. Treat 50/30/20 as a starting split that will not fit every household. Criteria 50/30/20 Zero-Based How income is split 50% needs, 30% wants, 20% savings and extra debt payments Every dollar assigned to spending, saving or debt until zero remains Hypothetical $4,000 example $2,000 needs, $1,200 wants, $800 savings and extra debt $2,150 bills, $600 groceries and transport, $350 minimums, $400 wants, $500 savings Fits when Your needs take 50% of take-home pay or less Your needs take more than 50%, or you want every dollar named Strains when High housing costs or heavy debt push needs past 50% You skip assigning some dollars, so the total no longer reaches zero Verdict Simpler first budget when needs fit in half your pay Better first budget when needs already take more than half Our pick for a first budget comes down to one division. Total your needs from step 2 and divide by your take-home pay. If the result is 50% or less, start with 50/30/20, because three shares are fewer numbers to track. If the result is above 50%, skip 50/30/20 and use a zero-based budget. Our answer would flip only if your needs later drop under half your pay, at which point the three-share split becomes the easier one to run. If your debts already exceed what your income can cover, a nonprofit credit counselor or a fee-only financial planner can review your specific situation before you pick either method. Fixed Costs, Flexible Costs and Pay-Yourself-First Timing Fixed costs go into your working budget first, and flexible costs fill in the space that remains. Fixed costs are bills like rent, insurance and minimum debt payments. Flexible costs are spending like food and fun, where the amount moves with your choices. Write the fixed costs down at their full amounts before you assign a single dollar to flexible categories. Whatever remains after fixed costs is the real limit for groceries, eating out and entertainment combined. If that remainder looks too small, try the Household Budget Calculator . Save a set amount on payday, before you spend, instead of saving whatever is left at the end of the month. Set up the transfer for the day your pay arrives, so the savings line in your budget happens first. Build a small cash cushion before you start paying debt down aggressively. Our guide on how much emergency fund you need covers how large that cushion should be. Once the cushion exists, debt snowball vs avalanche compares two ways to order your extra debt payments. A Bill Calendar for Tight Weeks A bill calendar lists every bill by due date, so you can spot the weeks when more money goes out than comes in. This is step 3 of the CFPB method, and it fixes a gap a monthly total hides. A budget can balance for the month and still come up short in the week before payday. Mark each payday on the same calendar as your bills. If two large bills land in the days before your next paycheck, set aside part of the earlier paycheck when it arrives. That way the money for those bills is sitting in your account on the due date. The CFPB notes that late or missed payments can affect your credit score. A calendar with every due date written down shows which weeks are tight. Add a reminder ahead of each due date so you can move money if the balance looks low. Why Budgets Fail in the First Three Months New budgets usually need two or three months of adjustment before the categories match how you spend. Expect that from the start, and treat a missed category as information for next month's numbers. Three problems can show up in that stretch, and each one has a fix: Categories set too tight. If groceries run over every week, raise that line and lower a looser category by the same amount, so the total still matches your income. Forgotten irregular costs. When a forgotten cost shows up, add it as its own category and set aside a share of it each month. No review. Pick a regular day to compare what you spent against each category. The CFPB advises updating your budget after a change in employment or in your spending habits. It gives no fixed review schedule, so treat a job change or a change in how you spend as your signal to revisit the four steps. If higher prices keep breaking your categories, our guide on how to budget when prices keep rising covers adjusting for that. If every month ends with nothing left no matter how you adjust, compare your income with your fixed costs. Our guide on how to stop living paycheck to paycheck works through that situation step by step. Which Calculator Fits the Way You Make a Budget Each budget calculator on ModernWallet matches a different situation, and you need the numbers from steps 1 and 2 before any of them gives a useful result. Pick the one that matches where you are: Building your first plan from a month of statements: the Monthly Budget Calculator . Wanting a quick overview of income against spending: the main Budget Calculator . Testing whether your needs fit in half your pay: the 50/30/20 Budget Calculator . Needs already above half your pay, or wanting every dollar named: the Zero-Based Budget Calculator . Budgeting for a whole household with several categories: the Household Budget Calculator . Living on a student income: the Student Budget Calculator , plus our guide on how to budget for teens and college students . Make your budget today: write down every income source from your latest pay stub, then enter it in the Monthly Budget Calculator . Frequently asked questions How do I make a budget if I have never had one? Follow the four CFPB steps in order: list your income, track a month of spending, put your bills on a calendar by due date, then build a working budget from those numbers. Start with your latest pay stub today, and use a month of bank and card statements for the spending step. What is the easiest budgeting method for beginners? The 50/30/20 split is the simpler method if your needs take half your take-home pay or less, because it has only three shares to track. If your needs take more than half, a zero-based budget fits better. Try the 50/30/20 Budget Calculator with your own numbers. How much of my income should go to savings in a budget? The 50/30/20 method puts 20% of take-home pay toward savings and debt payments beyond the minimums. Treat that as a starting split, since high housing costs or heavy debt can leave less room. A fee-only financial planner can tailor the savings share to your situation. How often should I update my budget? Update your budget whenever your employment or spending habits change, which is the trigger the CFPB names. The CFPB gives no fixed review schedule. In the first two or three months, expect to adjust categories as your real spending shows up. Should I budget by hand, in a spreadsheet or in an app? Use the format you will open every week. Any format works once it holds your income, a month of spending and your bill due dates. Sources We prioritize primary sources for rules, formulas, rates, limits, and definitions. This guide explains a simplified percentage framework scaled for a student budget, how to manage irregular income and aid disbursements, the two most common traps for first-time credit card and subscription users, and how to build an emergency fund habit before you need one. Tools for this journey 50/30/20 budget → Monthly budget → High-yield savings → Why a Student Budget Looks Different From an Adult Budget A student budget skips the biggest line items in a typical household budget, like a mortgage or a 401(k) contribution, and replaces them with costs unique to this stage of life. Dorm fees, a meal plan, textbooks, and splitting a lease with roommates take the place of rent and a full grocery budget. Income looks different too. Instead of one predictable paycheck, a student's money often comes from several irregular sources: a part-time job, a twice-a-year financial aid refund, or occasional support from family. Building a budget around a single "monthly income" number, the way an adult budget does, usually doesn't fit a student's real cash flow. The goal at this stage isn't a perfect budget — it's building the habit of tracking money in and out before the stakes get higher. Every habit built now carries forward into the bigger budgets that come with a first full-time job. Tracking Irregular Income: Paychecks, Aid Refunds, and Family Support Irregular income needs a different plan than a steady paycheck, because the same total dollars can either run out early or feel abundant depending on when they arrive. Start by listing every source separately: hourly pay from a job, any financial aid refund, and any recurring help from family. A financial aid refund is often the largest single deposit a student sees all semester, since it can include loan or grant money left over after tuition and fees are paid directly to the school. Treat that lump sum as money that has to stretch across the whole semester, not spending cash for the week it arrives — divide it by the number of weeks until the next expected deposit before deciding what's safe to spend. A part-time paycheck fluctuates with your scheduled hours, especially around exams when students often cut back their shifts. Use your lowest realistic pay period, not your best one, as the number your fixed costs — rent, phone bill, meal plan top-ups — are built around. A Simplified Percentage Framework Scaled for a Student Budget A percentage-based budget works well for students because it scales automatically with whatever income actually shows up that month. One common starting framework splits spending into needs, wants, and savings, a version of the 50/30/20 rule most people have heard of for a full household budget. Federal law requires every card statement to show a warning box explaining how much longer you'll carry the debt if you pay only the minimum, under rules the CFPB explains on its site. Is Robinhood Gold Worth It? By Jonathan Velez , Personal Finance Writer & Editor · Reviewed against primary sources · Updated October 29, 2026 Robinhood Gold is worth its $50 annual subscription if you hit any one of four break-even points: contributing at least $2,500 a year to an IRA, holding roughly $1,389 in uninvested cash, carrying $1,000 or more on margin, or keeping $120,000 or more in a Robinhood Strategies account. If your account does not hit one of those thresholds, the perks do not offset the subscription cost and you should stay on the free tier. At ModernWallet, we track financial products by running the cash math before looking at secondary features. The core subscription gives you an extra 2 percentage points of IRA match, a variable 3.6% annual percentage yield (APY) on idle cash through the High-Yield Cash Program as of September 17, 2026, an interest-free buffer on your first $1,000 of margin, larger instant deposits, and research tools. Whether that bundle makes financial sense depends on how you use your account. A passive investor who maxes out an annual IRA contribution can easily clear the $50 annual fee through the match alone. An active trader who uses margin or keeps cash waiting for dips can clear it on interest savings. But a casual stock buyer who deposits small sums into a taxable account and carries little cash will lose money on the subscription. Tools for this journey Roth IRA calculator → High-yield savings calculator → When Robinhood Gold Pays for Its $50 Fee Robinhood Gold pays for itself when any single perk returns more than the $50 annual subscription cost. Each Gold perk can clear the $50 fee on its own, so the table tests them one at a time. Benefit What It Is Worth Break-Even Point Extra 2% IRA Match $20 per $1,000 contributed $2,500 in annual IRA contributions Variable 3.6% Cash APY (as of Sept 17, 2026) $36 per $1,000 in cash a year Roughly $1,389 of uninvested cash $1,000 Interest-Free Margin $52.50 a year at the variable 5.25% rate (as of Sept 17, 2026) $1,000 carried on margin for a full year Robinhood Strategies Cap 0.25% fee waived above $100k $120,000 or more in managed assets The extra Individual Retirement Account (IRA) match is the fastest trigger for most long-term investors. Robinhood provides a 1% match on eligible contributions to all users, but Gold bumps that to 3%. That 2 percentage point bonus represents an extra $20 for every $1,000 you deposit. Once you contribute $2,500 during the tax year, that bonus hits exactly $50, which covers the annual subscription fee. You can model how those deposits compound inside a tax-sheltered account with our Roth IRA calculator . The cash APY break-even works on uninvested money sitting in your brokerage account. Through the Robinhood High-Yield Cash Program , Gold subscribers earn a variable 3.6% APY as of September 17, 2026. Because 3.6% of $1,388.89 equals $50, maintaining roughly $1,389 in idle cash across the year produces enough interest to offset the annual fee. Robinhood does not publish an APY for uninvested cash held by non-Gold members on the pages checked, so this calculation measures the absolute yield generated against the $50 cost. For investors holding more cash than that, you can check competing accounts on our roundup of the best brokerage accounts for interest on cash . The margin break-even appeals to investors who borrow against their equities. Robinhood Gold includes your first $1,000 of margin interest-free. At Robinhood 's variable 5.25% rate for balances up to $50,000 (as of September 17, 2026), borrowing that first $1,000 for twelve months would normally cost $52.50 in interest. The interest waiver alone saves you $52.50, clearing the $50 annual subscription by $2.50. The fourth path applies to Robinhood Strategies, the automated portfolio management product. Robinhood charges a 0.25% annual management fee on these accounts, but caps the fee at $250 per year for Gold members by waiving charges on balances above $100,000. Without Gold, a $200,000 Strategies balance incurs a $500 yearly fee. With Gold, you pay only the $250 cap plus the $50 subscription, saving $200 net. Robinhood Gold Billing and Cancellation Robinhood Gold costs $5 per month or $50 per year when billed annually. Choosing the annual plan saves $10 compared to paying $5 every month over a full calendar year. Robinhood states in its billing guide that subscription charges are deducted from your individual investing account at the beginning of each billing cycle. New subscribers can test the features using a one-time free trial for their first 30 days, as outlined on the Robinhood Gold landing page . If your account lacks enough buying power to cover the fee when the billing cycle rolls over, you risk an account deficit, a margin call if margin trading is turned on, or an automatic downgrade back to the standard tier. Cancelling your membership is handled directly inside the mobile app. You navigate to Account (the person icon), open the Menu (three horizontal bars), select Robinhood Gold, and tap Cancel membership. According to Robinhood's downgrading policy , all Gold features stay active through the conclusion of your current billing period. Once that cycle concludes, perks such as the High-Yield Cash Program are disabled. Two rules limit cancelling. First, if you opened a Robinhood Gold Credit Card, Robinhood requires you to close that credit card account before it lets you cancel your Gold membership. Second, cancelling Gold within 1 year of your first Gold IRA match triggers Robinhood 's Gold cancellation IRA match removal fee, which takes back the extra 2% match. Your next billing date is shown under Account → Menu → Robinhood Gold; cancel before it to avoid another charge. If another subscription has unclear billing or cancellation steps, use the subscription cancellation planner to map the route and keep proof. The Robinhood Gold IRA Match Rules and Requirements Robinhood offers an IRA match of 3% on eligible annual retirement contributions for Gold members, compared to 1% for standard users. For 2026, Robinhood lists IRA contribution limits of $7,500 under age 50 and $8,600 at 50 and older. If you max out your IRA at $7,500, a non-Gold user earns a $75 match, while a Gold user earns a $225 match. At age 50 or older, maxing out at $8,600 yields $86 without Gold versus $258 with Gold. In both cases, the extra 2% bonus provides $150 or $172 in additional funding, which far exceeds the $50 annual membership fee. This match comes with structural conditions detailed in the Robinhood IRA match rules . Direct account transfers from outside brokers and old 401(k) rollovers earn only a 1% match for everyone, regardless of whether you pay for Gold. Contributions from accounts managed by Robinhood Strategies are not eligible for the IRA match. Keeping the match depends on two time limits. First, matched funds must remain in your IRA for at least 5 years. Withdrawing early can trigger an early removal fee if your ending balance drops below the total matched deposit plus the earned match. Second, you must maintain an active Gold membership for at least 1 full year starting from the date of your first Gold match. If you cancel Gold before that 1-year mark, Robinhood assesses a cancellation fee equal to the extra 2% match. If your account lacks the uninvested cash to pay that charge, Robinhood reserves the right to liquidate your investment positions to recover the balance. Cash Yield and Margin Perks Under the Robinhood cash program terms , Gold subscribers earn a variable 3.6% APY as of September 17, 2026. This rate is subject to change at any time based on broader market conditions. Interest compounds daily and pays out monthly into your brokerage balance. There are no minimum balance requirements or maximum deposit caps tied to earning this APY. Margin trading features a $1,000 interest-free allowance for Gold members, which applies to one account with margin investing enabled. Beyond that initial $1,000 buffer, Robinhood charges tiered margin interest calculated daily on settled margin balances. As of September 17, 2026, those variable rates are: Up to $50,000: 5.25% $50,000 to $100,000: 5.05% $100,000 to $1,000,000: 4.75% $1,000,000 to $10,000,000: 4.50% $10,000,000 to $50,000,000: 4.45% Above $50,000,000: 4.20% Gold also raises how much of a deposit you can use instantly. As documented in Robinhood's instant deposit guidelines , standard accounts get instant access to deposits up to $1,000, or 2 times their portfolio value rounded down to the nearest thousand if greater. Gold raises standard taxable brokerage limits to $5,000, or 3 times your portfolio value if greater. These larger limits do not apply to retirement accounts; IRA instant deposits remain capped at $1,000 regardless of your Gold subscription status. To evaluate how these trading terms compare across platforms, you can see our Robinhood vs. Fidelity breakdown and our Robinhood vs. Webull comparison . Gold Research and AI Tools Robinhood Gold includes technical market data and fundamental equity analysis designed for self-directed taxable individual and joint accounts. Subscribers receive Level II Market Data powered by Nasdaq TotalView . This feed displays real-time depth of book with multiple bid and ask quotes. According to Robinhood 's market data disclosures, this view only includes quotes submitted by Nasdaq participants, meaning it does not capture order books from other trading venues or internal Robinhood flow. Fundamental research comes in the form of company reports from Morningstar . Robinhood first integrated Morningstar research and Nasdaq Level 2 data back in June 2019. For derivatives traders, Gold also lists a discounted index options fee of $0.35 per contract and a futures commission of $0.50 per contract. Gold also includes Cortex Digests. As described in Robinhood's Cortex documentation , these are AI-generated Asset Digests and Portfolio Digests written in plain language. Robinhood says these summaries are not formal research reports, recommendations, or personalized investment advice. If you are following recent platform updates regarding autonomous execution, read our guide on Robinhood agentic trading explained . No source ties Robinhood Agents to Gold. Downsides and Restrictions of a Gold Membership The main downside to Robinhood Gold is paying recurring fees for features that sit unused. Paying $50 a year or $5 a month drains your cash balance if you do not actively take advantage of the 3% IRA match, borrow on margin, or hold sufficient uninvested cash. The IRA match holds several structural risks. You must remain an active Gold subscriber for at least 1 full year to retain the bonus match, which commits you to at least $50 in Gold subscription fees. If you cancel early, Robinhood claws back the extra 2% match and may sell positions to cover the fee if you lack uninvested cash. Withdrawing matched funds within 5 years can trigger an early removal fee if your remaining balance falls below the matched deposit plus the match. Cash and margin rates are variable. The 3.6% cash APY and 5.25% base margin rate as of September 17, 2026, can drop or rise whenever market benchmark yields shift. If the cash APY declines, your break-even cash threshold increases. Finally, subscribers who sign up for the Robinhood Gold Card face an administrative barrier: Robinhood does not allow you to cancel your Gold subscription without shutting down your Gold Card first, creating friction if you decide you no longer want the paid software membership. Who Should Get Robinhood Gold and Who Should Skip It Robinhood Gold pays for itself for four kinds of Robinhood user and costs money for everyone else. For how Robinhood 's terms compare with other brokers, see our SoFi Invest vs. Robinhood comparison and our Charles Schwab vs. Robinhood review . Robinhood Gold makes financial sense for: - IRA investors depositing $2,500 or more annually, where the extra 2% match exceeds the $50 subscription fee. - Savers keeping more than $1,389 in uninvested cash who want a variable 3.6% APY as of September 17, 2026, compounding daily. - Traders who carry $1,000 of margin all year. - Investors with $120,000 or more in Robinhood Strategies, where the $250 fee cap saves more than the $50 subscription. You should skip Robinhood Gold if: - You invest small sums in a taxable account only. - You cannot commit to maintaining the Gold subscription for 12 months after receiving an IRA match. - You do not hold idle cash in your brokerage account and prefer to keep your emergency fund in a separate bank. - You are a beginner learning the basics of investing who might find Level II order books and margin unnecessary. Before upgrading, our guide on whether Robinhood is safe covers what protects the money in your account. The verdict changes if Robinhood lowers the Gold APY, changes the 3% IRA match, or raises the $50 price; rerun the four break-even points against the new figures. Add up your expected IRA contributions and idle cash, then compare the match and interest with the $50 fee. Frequently asked questions Is Robinhood Gold $50 a month? No. Robinhood Gold costs either $5 per month or $50 per year if you choose annual billing. The $50 figure represents the full annual membership cost, which saves you $10 compared to paying the $5 monthly rate for twelve months. At what point is Robinhood Gold worth it? Robinhood Gold is worth it once you reach any one of four break-even points: contributing at least $2,500 annually to an IRA, holding roughly $1,389 or more in uninvested cash at the variable 3.6% APY as of September 17, 2026, borrowing at least $1,000 on margin to save $52.50 in interest, or keeping $120,000 or more in a Robinhood Strategies account. Are there any downsides to Robinhood Gold? Yes. Downsides include paying $50 annually for unused perks, variable cash APY and margin rates that can fluctuate, a 1-year Gold membership requirement to keep the full 3% IRA match, a 5-year holding rule on matched IRA deposits, and a policy requiring you to close the Robinhood Gold Card before cancelling Gold. How hard is it to cancel Robinhood Gold? Cancelling takes a few taps inside the mobile app by going to Account, selecting Menu, choosing Robinhood Gold, and tapping Cancel membership. Your benefits run until the end of the current billing cycle. However, if you have an open Robinhood Gold Card, you must close that credit card before the app permits cancellation. Gold boosts your IRA contribution match from 1% to 3%. On a $2,500 contribution, that extra 2 percentage points equals exactly $50, fully paying for the annual subscription.
